newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Haughey's lawyer wins cash probe adjournment.
newsitem.headline: Haughey's lawyer wins cash probe adjournment.

text.p: Lawyers for former Irish Prime Minister Charles Haughey won an adjournment on Monday of hearings of charges that he was given handouts of more than a million pounds (dollars) by department store tycoon Ben Dunne.
Lawyer Eoin McGonigal told a tribunal that hearings of evidence should be adjourned until the collection of testimony into the allegations was complete.

Justice Brian McCracken said that evidence, "almost entirely of a banking nature," was being collected in London and elsewhere and adjourned the hearing of evidence which was to have been given by Noel Smyth, Dunne's solicitor.

It was the first time that Haughey, Prime Minister four times between 1979 and 1992, had been represented at the tribunal, which is investigating payments by businessman Dunne to politicians of all major political parties.

The investigation has raised calls for a new code governing relations between business and politics and drawn major media coverage in the runup to what is expected to be an early general election in June.

For the first time members of the public queued to get into the week-old hearings in the hope of seeing the reclusive Haughey, once one of the most powerful figures in the Fianna Fail political party.

Last week Dunne testified that he had given Haughey a total of 1.3 million pounds over several years, most of it channelled to offshore bank accounts and 200,000 pounds in bank drafts he personally handed over to the former premier.
Dunne, who was dropped by his family from the board of the Dunne's Stores retail chain in 1993, told the tribunal he gave money to all major political parties to help them out with election expenses.
But he said the money for Haughey was to help him out of financial difficulties as he understood the one-time Prime Minister was "a bit skint (broke)."
Smyth said last Friday he had met Haughey five times recently in connection with the payments and was to have given evidence about the meetings on Monday.
Prime Minister John Bruton testified to the tribunal on Monday that Dunne gave his Fine Gael party 50,000 pounds in 1991 but said no political favours were asked or given.

Dunne has also revealed that he gave the Labour party led by Dick Spring the current Foreign Minister, 50,000 pounds for a theme park project as well as cash to fund the election campaign of President Mary Robinson.

Spring, Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, Health Minister Michael Noonan and a host of other leading political figures have all given testimony to the tribunal, which is expected to adjourn in the near future.
